Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

Arun sat in the environmental control station with three screens open and a tray of cold protein bars he had not touched.

The numbers on the left screen were the problem.

Tank pressure. Tank volume. Gas composition. Leak rate. Crew consumption. Sabatier output. Electrolysis yield. Reserve margin.

He had run the projection fourteen times in the last six hours. Each time the answer came back the same: comfortable now, uncomfortable later.

The base had seventy-two days of oxygen at current consumption. That assumed perfect recycling from the Sabatier reactor, which was not a safe assumption. It assumed no major leaks, which was a worse one. It assumed they kept the pressure at 55 kilopascals, which was the minimum for breathable air and already made everyone feel slightly winded during hard work.

Seventy-two days sounded like a lot until you thought about it in the right units. It was two and a half months. It was ten weeks until every tank in the base read zero. Ten weeks until every person in the linked modules started suffocating in their sleep.

Arun had been an environmental systems engineer for twelve years. He had passed hundreds of simulations, written protocols for a dozen failure modes, trained on the oxygen-loop mockup at Johnson Space Center until he could rebuild a CO₂ scrubber blindfolded. None of that training had prepared him for the moment when the spreadsheet showed him exactly how far the bottom was.

He pulled up the consumption graph. The colony was breathing roughly nine kilograms of oxygen per person per day. That was more than Earth because of the lower pressure. More oxygen per breath because the partial pressure had to be maintained. Twenty-one people meant roughly a hundred and ninety kilograms of O₂ consumed every day. The tanks held thirteen thousand kilograms.

Seventy-two days.

Then the numbers changed if the Sabatier dipped. Or if the electrolysis stack lost efficiency. Or if someone opened an airlock for too long during an EVA transition.

Seventy-two days could become sixty-six.

Could become fifty.

He pushed the tray of protein bars aside and stood up. The module smelled like recycled air. It always smelled like recycled air. That was the thing about closed-loop life support—you could never quite scrub the smell of yourself out of the air no matter how good the filters were.

Arun walked through the connecting tunnel toward the mess. The tunnel was twenty meters of ribbed fabric that flexed slightly when the pressure differential shifted. He had stopped noticing the flex during the first week. Now he barely noticed the sound of his own footsteps on the metal grating.

Jonah was in the mess, drinking water from a bulb and staring at a tablet.

"Oxygen," Arun said.

Jonah looked up. "What about it?"

"We have enough for now. Not enough for forever."

"How much is enough for now?"

"Seventy-two days. Call it fifty-two with safety factor."

Jonah set the bulb down. "That's tight."

"It's survivable if everything works perfectly. Nothing works perfectly."

"You're not telling me you want to cut the Sabatier temperature again."

"No. I want to stop thinking about reserves and start thinking about production."

Jonah leaned back. The chair creaked. Everything on Mars creaked after the first week. The temperature cycling and the pressure and the thin, dry air found every joint and seal and made them complain.

"Production from what?" Jonah said. "We brought one flight-grade oxygen unit. It's a breadboard. A toy."

"I know."

"How much does it make?"

"Three hundred grams per day. Maybe four hundred on a good power cycle."

"Oxygen," Arun said.

Elena looked up. "I saw your projection. Seventy-two days."

"Fifty-two with safety factor."

"I read the whole spreadsheet."

"Then you know we need a bigger plant."

Elena leaned back. The seat creaked. Everything on Mars creaked.

"The flight unit is a prototype," she said. "It was meant to validate the technology. Not to sustain us."

"I know."

Elena looked at Jonah. "You've been thinking about this."

"I've been drawing it. Since about twenty-two hundred hours."

"Draw it for me now."

Power budget. Thermal management. He talked for fifteen minutes without stopping. When he finished, Elena sat in silence.

"Seventeen kilowatts continuous," she said finally.

"Yes."

"That's not a small ask."

"I know."

"If this fails, we lose a significant fraction of our power budget for the duration of the build plus the test run. We lose workshop hours that could go to other critical systems. We lose morale."

"If it works," Arun said, "we stop counting down. We start counting up."

Elena looked at him. Her eyes were red at the edges. She had been sleeping in shifts, like everyone else. But her voice was steady.

"What's your confidence level?"

Arun hesitated. That was the question he had been avoiding all night.

"I'm confident the chemistry works," he said. "Solid oxide electrolysis is proven technology. The Martian atmosphere is consistent. The compressor geometry is straightforward."

"But?"

Elena turned to Jonah. "What's your gut say?"

"Two shots," Elena said.

"Two shots."

The base was alive around them, breathing and drinking and thinking, and every system depended on decisions made in this tiny room.

"Authorize the build," Elena said.

Jonah exhaled. He had not realized he was holding his breath.

"Full workshop priority," Elena continued. "You can reassign whatever labor and tools you need. But I want a written plan within twelve hours. Power budget. Timeline. Risk register. Failure contingency. If this thing breaks, I want to know exactly what we lose before we start."

"You'll have it by oh-seven-hundred."

"I want Arun on thermal modeling full-time. No other duties until the stack design is locked."

"I'll pull the data tonight," Arun said.

Elena nodded. She looked at the two of them for a long moment.

"We're running out of Earth," she said. "Every system we rely on came from the ships. Every replacement part, every consumable, every margin. This plant is the first thing we build that has to work because the imported version won't last. If we get it right, we breathe. If we get it wrong—"

She did not finish the sentence. She did not need to.

Jonah and Arun left the command module together. The corridor was dim, lit only by emergency strips. The base was on night cycle. Most of the crew was asleep.

"She's right about the risk," Arun said quietly.

"I know."

"If this fails, we don't just lose the power. We lose the confidence that we can solve our own problems. That's harder to replace than a ceramic stack."

Jonah stopped walking. He turned to face Arun in the dim light.

"Then we don't fail."

It was not a boast. It was not a promise. It was a statement of intent, stripped of all decoration, spoken by a man who had spent his entire life making things work in places where things did not want to work.

Arun looked at him.

"Seventy-two days," he said.

"Seventy-two days to build a factory that turns poison into air."

They stood in the corridor for a moment longer. The ventilation fans cycled. The base hummed. Outside, the Martian atmosphere drifted past the habitat walls at six hundred pascals, ninety-five percent carbon dioxide, waiting for someone to take it apart and make it useful.

Jonah turned and walked toward the workshop.

Arun watched him go.

Then he went back to the environmental station to run the thermal models one more time, because running them one more time was the only thing he could do until the sun came up and the welding started.

The sun would come up in four hours.

There was a lot of work to do.
